frontmatter.subtitle: How a computer turns sound into information

children.value: is how a computer turns audio into information, and it includes many of the other things we have talked about in this book: what does a machine need from acoustics, from psychoacoustics, from music theory, before it can say anything about a recording? This includes overviews of signal processing and machine learning but we will also briefly look at how the chain can be reversed to generate music. What is important to remember is that, unlike humans, a machine works entirely on numbers.

, turns sound, whether music, speech or a soundscape, into structured information. The steps are the same for each: capture the audio, extract features that reflect how we hear, find events and boundaries, attach labels, and present the result.
Machine listening is the foundation of
(MIR), a field focused on asking musical questions of recordings, and of today’s musical AI

As in the rest of the book, the examples below are generated with Python code, and many use the librosa audio processing library. These are standard tools in the MIR community. You are not expected to learn them in this course, but it is good to know the names.
Dig deeper: Python, Jupyter, and librosa
is a programming language widely used for scientific computing, data analysis, and machine learning. Most of its power comes from libraries: general scientific ones (
). Its clean syntax makes it quick to learn, and it runs almost anywhere.

is a web-based document that mixes live code, text, figures, and results. Code sits in cells that run one at a time, with the output shown under each, which suits exploring data step by step and sharing the result. Notebooks support several languages (Python, R, Julia) and export to HTML and PDF. This book is written as Jupyter Notebooks.
, a general-purpose Python library for audio and music analysis.

In the following, we will assume that we already have an audio recording in place. From that, we will look at a pipeline in four stages: cleaning the audio, extracting features, separating sources, and finding events and sections.
Audio reaches the machine the way

described it: through a signal from a microphone to one or more converters to be stored as a file of numbers. Before moving on to analysis, the file is usually resampled to a common sampling rate, normalised in level, and cleaned of hum and clicks, so that recordings become comparable and the later stages behave the same on each.

import librosa
from IPython.display import Audio, display
import librosa.display
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})

audio_path = "audio/week6_audio_ex_2_coltrane_myfavthings.mp3"
y, sr = librosa.load(audio_path, sr=22050, mono=True)

hop_length = 512

# Waveform (separate figure)
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3.3))
try:
    librosa.display.waveshow(y, sr=sr)
except AttributeError:
    librosa.display.waveplot(y, sr=sr)
plt.title('Waveform')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Amplitude')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# show a playbar for the loaded audio below the spectrogram
display(Audio(audio_path))

# Spectrogram (STFT -> dB) (separate figure)
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3.3))
S = np.abs(librosa.stft(y, n_fft=2048, hop_length=hop_length))
S_db = librosa.amplitude_to_db(S, ref=np.max)
librosa.display.specshow(S_db, sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length, x_axis='time', y_axis='log', cmap='magma')
plt.title('Spectrogram (STFT, log-frequency)')
plt.ylabel('Frequency (Hz)')
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.colorbar(label='dB')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Figure: The running example, an excerpt of John Coltrane’s My Favorite Things: the waveform (top) and its log-frequency spectrogram (bottom), with the audio between them.

Let us now consider how we can extract some features from the example above.
Estimating the tempo of a song is not straightforward, and can be challenging also for humans if there are many tempo changes and ambiguous metres. We start by creating a
, which shows which tempi are prominent at each moment:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})

# Tempogram (rhythmic autocorrelation)
onset_env = librosa.onset.onset_strength(y=y, sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length)
tempogram = librosa.feature.tempogram(onset_envelope=onset_env, sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3.3))
librosa.display.specshow(tempogram, sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length, x_axis='time', y_axis='tempo', cmap='magma')
plt.colorbar(label='Autocorrelation')
plt.title('Tempogram (local tempo over time)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Figure: Tempogram of the excerpt: the strength of each tempo (vertical axis, in BPM) at each moment, computed by autocorrelation of the onset curve.

The tempogram is hard to read directly, and also reflects the complexity of the music in question. To try to estimate the perceived tempo, we can smooth the tempogram and average across the bands to get a single running tempo estimate:

from librosa.feature import rhythm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})

times = librosa.frames_to_time(np.arange(len(onset_env)), sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length)
tempo_est = librosa.feature.tempo(onset_envelope=onset_env, sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length)
# Instantaneous tempo: the strongest tempo in a short (2 s) autocorrelation window around each frame.
# The default window is 8 s, which already averages so much that smoothing it again changes nothing.
tempo_running = rhythm.tempo(onset_envelope=onset_env, sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length, aggregate=None, ac_size=2.0)

# Smooth the running estimate with a moving average of about 2 s
win = int(round(2.0 * sr / hop_length)) | 1
kernel = np.ones(win) / win
tempo_smooth = np.convolve(tempo_running, kernel, mode='same')

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3.3))
plt.plot(times, tempo_running, color='gray', alpha=0.5, linewidth=0.8, label='Instantaneous tempo (2 s window)')
plt.plot(times, tempo_smooth, color='C1', linewidth=2, label='Smoothed running tempo (2 s moving average)')
plt.axhline(float(tempo_est[0]), color='k', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label=f'Global tempo: {tempo_est[0]:.2f} BPM')

# Optionally mark beat times
if 'beat_times' in globals():
    for bt in beat_times:
        plt.axvline(bt, color='r', linestyle=':', alpha=0.25, linewidth=0.8)

plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Tempo (BPM)')
plt.title('Running estimated tempo (per-frame) with smoothed curve')
plt.legend(loc='upper right')
plt.xlim(times[0], times[-1])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Figure: The strongest tempo in a 2 s window around each frame (grey), the same smoothed with a 2 s moving average (orange), the global estimate (dashed) and the detected beats (dotted).

As you can see, the instantaneous tempo varies, as in any real performance. But we are looking for the general tempo for the whole segment, so we calculate the average of all the values. The estimate is close to what a listener would say, but it is an average over a passage whose tempo moves, and a tempogram can as easily settle on half or double the felt tempo (the
), so it is a starting point for the ear, not a verdict.

: the onset curve is compared with a delayed copy of itself, and the delays at which the two match are the periods of the beat and its subdivisions. The same idea finds pitch. Autocorrelate the waveform itself, and the delay at which it best matches is the period of the fundamental, whose inverse is the frequency. Pitch and tempo are the same kind of thing, a periodicity, at different speeds: a tempo lies between about 0.5 and 5 cycles per second, a pitch between 20 and 20,000, which is what the

demonstrated. Pitch trackers such as pYIN add a model for choosing between the candidate periods when several match, and give the pitch contours listed among the mid-level features above. Harmony is found the other way round, from the spectrum rather than from delays: the chromagram folds the spectrum into twelve pitch classes, and a key profile compares that distribution with templates for the major and minor keys, as the key estimate printed under the chromagram shows.
To estimate the pitch of a tune, the key it is played in and the harmonies used, we can turn to the
, which estimates how much energy falls on each of the twelve pitch classes.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})
# Compute chromagram (CQT-based)
chroma = librosa.feature.chroma_cqt(y=y, sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3.3))
librosa.display.specshow(chroma, y_axis='chroma', x_axis='time', sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length, cmap='magma')
plt.colorbar(label='Chroma energy')
plt.title('Chromagram (CQT)')
plt.tight_layout()
# show the plot and an audio playbar for the loaded file
plt.show()
Figure: Chromagram of the excerpt: the energy in each of the twelve pitch classes over time.

From the chromagram, we can see that most of its energy is centred around a tone corresponding to pitch class E. Remember that a chromagram (like a spectrogram) is a visualisation of a collection of numbers. Calculating the averages of each “strip” in the chromagram, we can get a numerical value for how much they are represented, and, as you can see below, the E turns up as the one with the highest chroma energy. Remember that this is not in itself a proof that the note E is the most prominent, but it is a good indication. The printed key estimate goes one step further: it correlates the mean chroma with the major and minor key profiles from
, in every transposition, and reports the best match.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})
pitch_names = ['C', 'C#', 'D', 'D#', 'E', 'F', 'F#', 'G', 'G#', 'A', 'A#', 'B']
chroma_mean = chroma.mean(axis=1)
mean_chroma = chroma_mean

# Key estimate: correlate the mean chroma with the Krumhansl and Kessler (1982) major and minor
# key profiles in all twelve transpositions and report the best match
major = np.array([6.35, 2.23, 3.48, 2.33, 4.38, 4.09, 2.52, 5.19, 2.39, 3.66, 2.29, 2.88])
minor = np.array([6.33, 2.68, 3.52, 5.38, 2.60, 3.53, 2.54, 4.75, 3.98, 2.69, 3.34, 3.17])
scores = {f"{pitch_names[k]} {mode}": float(np.corrcoef(mean_chroma, np.roll(profile, k))[0, 1])
          for mode, profile in (("major", major), ("minor", minor)) for k in range(12)}
best = max(scores, key=scores.get)
print(f"Key estimate: {best} (correlation {scores[best]:.2f}; runner-up "
      f"{sorted(scores, key=scores.get)[-2]} at {sorted(scores.values())[-2]:.2f})")

idx = int(np.argmax(mean_chroma))
prominent = pitch_names[idx]
prominence = float(mean_chroma[idx])

# simple bar plot highlighting the most prominent class
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 2.5))
bars = plt.bar(pitch_names, mean_chroma, color='C0')
bars[idx].set_color('C1')
plt.ylabel('Mean chroma energy')
plt.title('Mean chroma per pitch class - highlighted = most prominent')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The chromagram can also help us to get information about the harmonic content of a tune. From the chromagram, we can see that the B also scores high. There are two reasons for this. First, from
, you would expect a high level of energy in the fundamental frequency (E) and its first overtones (the first being the E one octave above, and the second the B).

The second explanation for the prominent B in the chromagram is the music arrangement: B is present in both the E minor and the E major chord, the bass vamp moves between E and B, and McCoy Tyner’s piano voicings are built in fourths around B, E and A rather than in thirds. The chromagram therefore sees B both as an overtone of E and as a note played in its own right. The printed key estimate agrees on E, and major and minor come out close because the arrangement alternates between the two.

Notice that the third-highest pitch class in the example above is D#. This can partly be explained harmonically: Coltrane’s arrangement alternates an E minor vamp with an E major one, and over the major chord the piano adds the major seventh, D#, which also appears in the melody there.

There is one more explanation for the D#, which relates to the feature extraction method: the chroma bins are a semitone wide and D# sits next to E, the strongest bin, so the vibrato and the slightly flat intonation of the soprano saxophone spill some of E’s energy into D#. Running the same analysis on the harmonic part of the signal alone gives the same ordering, so this is pitched energy, not percussion.

G and G# are the lowest of all, although they are the thirds of both E minor and E major and therefore the first notes a music theorist would write down. There are two reasons for this as well. First, the voicings in fourths leave the third out most of the time. Second, when a third is played the time is split between G, in the minor passages, and G#, in the major ones, so each gets about half of an already small share. The middle group, A, F# and D, are the fourth, the second and the seventh of E: the notes of the fourth-based voicings and of the melody.

What is important to take from all of this is that a chromagram measures energy per pitch class, not chord membership. It reflects the harmonic series and the voicings as much as the chord symbols, which is why a key read off a chromagram has to be taken with the same care as the tempo estimate above.

In the example above, we examined the signal as one “chunk” of information. An alternative, and more advanced, approach is to begin by isolating individual instruments or voices from a mix, what is called
. Humans can do this easily: attend to one instrument in an ensemble or one voice in a crowd, as discussed in
. For machines the problem is not solved, and is actively researched in the MIR community.
A simple type of source separation is to split the signal into two parts: harmonic and percussive.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})
y_harmonic, y_percussive = librosa.effects.hpss(y)

fig, (ax_o, ax_hp) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
librosa.display.waveshow(y, sr=sr, ax=ax_o, color="0.4")
ax_o.set(title="Original waveform", ylabel="Amplitude", xlabel="")
librosa.display.waveshow(y_harmonic, sr=sr, ax=ax_hp, color="#1f77b4", alpha=0.9)
librosa.display.waveshow(y_percussive, sr=sr, ax=ax_hp, color="#d62728", alpha=0.7)
ax_hp.set(title="Harmonic and percussive components", ylabel="Amplitude", xlabel="Time (s)")
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
ax_hp.legend(handles=[mpatches.Patch(color="#1f77b4", label="Harmonic"),
                      mpatches.Patch(color="#d62728", label="Percussive")], loc="upper right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

display(Audio(y_harmonic, rate=sr))
display(Audio(y_percussive, rate=sr))
Figure: The excerpt’s waveform (top) and its harmonic and percussive components after harmonic–percussive separation (bottom). The two components can be heard below.
Signal-processing methods like this are well understood and help us along the way, but are still far from extracting each instrument fully. Nowadays, the state-of-the-art separators are
systems that have learned what voices, drums and bass sound like from large collections of recordings. Below is the result of using

, an open-source neural network trained on studio multitracks to separate the Coltrane track into the six stem types it is trained on: drums, bass, vocals, guitar, piano, and everything else. You can see the result here and listen to each extracted stem:

import os
import numpy as np
import librosa, librosa.display
from IPython.display import Audio, display
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
if "y" not in globals():          # so that this cell also runs on its own
    y, sr = librosa.load("audio/week6_audio_ex_2_coltrane_myfavthings.mp3", sr=22050, mono=True)
    hop_length = 512
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})

stem_dir = "audio/coltrane_stems"
stems = ["drums", "bass", "piano", "other", "vocals", "guitar"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(stems), 1, figsize=(10, 10), sharex=True)
for ax, name in zip(axes, stems):
    y_s, sr_s = librosa.load(os.path.join(stem_dir, name + ".mp3"), sr=sr, mono=True)
    S_s = librosa.amplitude_to_db(np.abs(librosa.stft(y_s, n_fft=2048, hop_length=hop_length)), ref=np.max(np.abs(librosa.stft(y, n_fft=2048, hop_length=hop_length))))
    librosa.display.specshow(S_s, sr=sr, hop_length=hop_length, x_axis="time", y_axis="log", cmap="magma", ax=ax, vmin=-80, vmax=0)
    rms = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(y_s ** 2)))
    ax.set_ylabel(name)
    ax.text(0.99, 0.9, f"RMS {20 * np.log10(rms + 1e-9):.0f} dB", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="top", fontsize=8, color="w")
    ax.label_outer()
axes[0].set_title("Demucs (htdemucs_6s) stems of the Coltrane excerpt, log-frequency spectrograms on one colour scale")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

for name in stems:
    print(name)
    display(Audio(os.path.join(stem_dir, name + ".mp3")))
Figure: Log-frequency spectrograms of the six Demucs stems of the excerpt, on one colour scale, with a player for each stem below.

You can see/hear that the bass, piano and drum stems work quite well. The bass stem holds the E–B vamp, the piano stem the fourth-based voicings with B, E and A on top, and the drum stem the cymbals and brushes. The problem is that the Demucs model is not trained on saxophone sound, so the saxophone ends up in the “other” category with whatever else did not fit. The model extracts “vocals”, but since there are no vocals, that one is silent, and the “guitar” stem is also nearly silent, holding only some misclassified fragments of bass notes and piano chords. The lesson to learn from this is that a separator can only sort sound into the categories it was trained on.
To exemplify the importance of picking the right model, let us also investigate the result of another separator.

, a transformer that works on frequency bands and currently scores highest on the standard benchmark, is trained to split a mix into vocals and everything else. Run on the excerpt, its vocals stem is empty, about 50 dB below the mix, and its instrumental stem is the mix:

The model might have mistaken the saxophone for a voice, but it did not, which is correct. It is nevertheless useless on this music. BS-RoFormer works well for karaoke tracks, separating the voice from the rest, and fails on most other things.
Optional: separate a track into stems
While open source tools may be difficult to set up on your own, you can easily sign up for a free account on one of the commercial services, like

. Try to upload a track of your choice and see what you get. Where do you hear distortion, bleed between stems, or missing frequencies? How useful would these stems be for transcription or timing analysis, and what does that say about the limits of current separation?
Stem separation can be seen as a way of segmenting the sound “vertically”. Now, let us consider also “horizontal” segmentation, what is often called
: onsets, beats, the start of a chorus. This is the machine’s version of the grouping problem posed in
: which parts of a continuous signal belong together? While the auditory system handles event detection effortlessly, it is not at all straightforward for machines.
One classic method for event detection compares the recording with itself in a

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 9,
    "figure.figsize": (10, 4),
    "figure.dpi": 100,
    "savefig.dpi": 150,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})
# Compute and plot a self-similarity matrix using chroma frame features
X_feat = chroma.T  # shape: (n_frames, n_pitches)

# L2-normalize frame vectors (avoid division by zero)
norms = np.linalg.norm(X_feat, axis=1, keepdims=True)
norms[norms == 0] = 1.0
Xn = X_feat / norms

# Cosine self-similarity (frames x frames)
ssm = np.dot(Xn, Xn.T)

# Plot the self-similarity matrix mapped to time (uses `times` array already in the notebook)
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
extent = [times[0], times[-1], times[0], times[-1]]  # map indices to seconds
plt.imshow(ssm, origin='lower', aspect='auto', cmap='magma', extent=extent, vmin=0, vmax=1)
plt.xlabel('Time (s)')
plt.ylabel('Time (s)')
plt.title('Self-similarity matrix (cosine) - chroma/frame features')

# Optionally overlay beat times if available
if 'beat_times' in globals():
    for bt in beat_times:

Comparing the parts to describe the musical form takes more code and more judgement, so we will not continue with that here. What is important to understand is that machine listening gives fast, consistent and reproducible descriptions of acoustic properties. But it does not give musical interpretation. So you always need to check that what the machine suggests makes sense.

So far, we have only asked the machine to extract features and describe them. It can also try to answer: is this a trumpet, which genre, which song, will this listener like it? These are the classic tasks of MIR:
: which instrument, which genre, speech or music. The pitfalls are biased datasets and instruments that sound alike.
: audio features combined with listening behaviour. Useful for discovery, prone to bias, and hungry for personal data.
: audio into notes. Single melodies work well; full polyphonic transcription does not yet.
: verses, choruses, boundaries. “Meaningful” is subjective, so evaluation needs human judgement.
: “find tracks with a trumpet solo”. The hard part is mapping everyday words to reliable labels.
: estimating how music feels. This is where MIR meets the music psychology of
, with all the individual and cultural differences that chapter described.
Can you think of any examples of how these techniques are implemented in systems you use?

. They rely on specifying various rules as algorithms using thresholds, peak picking, and different types of decision rules. Such systems are small, fast, easy to understand and easy to tune, but they do not scale well and break when the music is unlike what they were tuned on.
The AI revolution is based on the capacities of

systems, which find their own patterns in data. When trained on enough data, they have proven to be more accurate and capable of solving also tasks they were not trained on. However, the downside is that they need to be trained on lots of data and require large computational resources. Also, they effectively function as a “black box”, meaning that it is impossible to know what they actually “think”. We use quotation marks here, since even though the machine may appear to think, machine learning is only fancy statistics.
Most learning-based systems are built from
(ANNs). Recall that we mentioned this when discussing

. Artificial neural networks were developed from the 1950s, inspired by the human brain. Such a network is made of simple units arranged in layers. Each unit multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up, passes the sum through a simple non-linear function, and hands the result to the next layer.

children.value: A simple artificial neural network: an input layer, one hidden layer and an output layer, each unit connected to every unit in the next layer by a weight.

Training means showing the network many examples, measuring how wrong its output is, and adjusting every weight a little towards being less wrong. By repeating this thousands, or even millions of times, the network “learns”.

is also based on artificial neural networks, but includes many more layers, which is why it is called “deep”. The idea is that early layers pick up local detail (a transient, a spectral edge) and later layers combine it into something abstract (a timbre, a chord, a genre).

What is important to understand is that the features emerging from such a network are not chosen by a person, and may not even be easily explained. Also, as we saw in the example above, what the network is trained on influences what it can find. If it is not trained to classify saxophone sounds, it will not find them by itself.
There are many different types of models. These are some of the more well-known model families:

describe a signal as moving between a small set of hidden states, such as notes or chords, and estimate the most likely state sequence. They are lightweight and work with little data, but struggle when musical patterns stretch over long spans.

networks process a sequence one step at a time, with LSTMs adding an internal memory for longer context. They handle moderate musical context well but are slower than models that process a whole sequence at once.
Temporal or dilated convolutional networks (temporal CNNs, TCNs) apply the pattern-matching filters of a
along the time axis, with deeper layers seeing longer stretches of signal. They compute efficiently and suit low-latency streaming, but the amount of context they see is fixed by the design.

let every moment in a sequence relate directly to every other, which suits long-range structure and tasks such as transcription and form analysis. They often give the best results but demand far more computation and memory, especially for long recordings.
AI-based systems can be rule-based or learning-based (or hybrid), but they can also differ in terms of how they operate in time. Most systems work in non-real-time, and are often referred to as

systems. Think of regular chatbots and other systems where you type in something and then get a result. They can be quite fast, but you never know exactly when the reply comes. This is fine for many use cases, including music analysis. Then, the system can look ahead, revise earlier decisions and run expensive smoothing, which is why transcription and structural analysis are done offline. Musical structure is easiest to find after the fact.
For music performance, however, one needs a system that can respond in
while the music plays, as in live accompaniment or an interactive installation. It hears only what has arrived and has a few tens of milliseconds to decide.
, the delay of a signal, is critical for such systems, and algorithms are typically developed to be simple and quick. A rapid response time is usually more important than the quality of the answer.
Dig deeper: where the latency comes from
Latency ≈ window duration + model lookahead + processing time. With
, the analysis window alone is ≈ 92.9 ms, and a
of 512 advances in 23.2 ms steps, so even before any model runs, the system is already that far behind the sound.

Real-time work therefore requires causal algorithms (causal filters, causal convolutions, stateful RNNs/TCNs, or streaming transformers with limited lookahead), a streaming frontend with short windows and small hops, cheap incremental features (onset strength, low-band log-mel, incremental CQT), and simple online post-processing (peak picking, adaptive thresholds). Compute has to be bounded and predictable to meet deployment constraints (CPU/GPU, battery, I/O), which in practice means lightweight models or hybrid pipelines with a rule-based front end and a small learned model.

Offline systems can instead use larger windows, global context, and bidirectional models (bi-RNNs, full attention), plus expensive post-processing (Viterbi smoothing, global segmentation, search) and whole-track normalisation.
We have so far focused on analytical machine listening systems, extracting information from music that already exists, or deciding something about it.
turns the pipeline around and produces new music
. The two are related: a system can only generate convincingly in a style it has learned to represent, and generative models reuse the model families described above.
or score-based generation works with notes: it produces notation or MIDI that a musician or a synthesiser then plays.
generation skips the score and produces the waveform directly. Some people think this can only work on big servers, but the three examples below were all made on a laptop with open-source software.
The oldest generative model is also the simplest. A
reads a tune note by note and counts how often each note follows the few notes before it.
and Isaacson used such chains for the fourth movement of the
in 1957, the first substantial piece composed with a computer
The example below learns from a few hundred German folk songs in the Essen Folksong Collection

. Each tune is first transposed to C major, so that the chain learns scale degrees rather than absolute pitches. The chain then counts, for every pair of consecutive notes, which note with which duration came next. Then, the generator walks through those counts: start as a tune in the collection starts, draw each next note in proportion to how often it followed the previous two, refuse any duration that would cross a barline, and stop after eight bars on the tonic. The result is rendered as notation with
and played with a plain synthetic tone:

import os, random, subprocess
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
import numpy as np
from IPython.display import Audio, display
from music21 import corpus, interval, pitch

# 1. Learn: the major-mode tunes of one Essen collection (Boehme's German folk songs), transposed to C major
opus = corpus.parse("essenFolksong/boehme10")
DURATIONS = {4.0: "1", 3.0: "2.", 2.0: "2", 1.5: "4.", 1.0: "4", 0.75: "8.", 0.5: "8", 0.25: "16"}
tunes = []
for s in opus.scores:
    k = s.analyze("key")
    if k.mode != "major":
        continue
    semis = interval.Interval(k.tonic, pitch.Pitch("C4")).semitones % 12
    shift = interval.Interval(semis if semis <= 6 else semis - 12)
    events = [(n.pitch.transpose(shift).midi, float(n.quarterLength))
              for n in s.parts[0].flatten().notes if n.isNote and float(n.quarterLength) in DURATIONS]
    if len(events) > 8:
        tunes.append(events)

ORDER = 2                                   # how many previous notes the chain remembers
table = defaultdict(Counter)                # (previous notes) -> Counter of next (pitch, duration)
starts = []
for ev in tunes:
    starts.append(tuple(ev[:ORDER]))
    for j in range(ORDER, len(ev)):
        table[tuple(ev[j - ORDER:j])][ev[j]] += 1
print(f"Learned from {len(tunes)} major-mode tunes: {len(table)} contexts, "
      f"{sum(sum(c.values()) for c in table.values())} transitions.")

# 2. Generate eight bars of 4/4 that end on the tonic; a note may not cross a barline
def generate(seed, bars=8):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    while True:
        out = list(rng.choice(starts))
        pos = sum(d for _, d in out)
        while pos < bars * 4:
            room = 4 - (pos % 4)
            options = [(e, w) for e, w in table.get(tuple(out[-ORDER:]), {}).items() if e[1] <= room]
            if not options:
                break
            e = rng.choices([e for e, _ in options], weights=[w for _, w in options])[0]
            out.append(e)
            pos += e[1]
        if pos == bars * 4 and out[-1][0] % 12 == 0:
            return out

tune = generate(seed=3)
print(f"Generated {len(tune)} notes.")

# 3. Notation with LilyPond (the book's notation renderer)
NAMES = ["c", "cis", "d", "dis", "e", "f", "fis", "g", "gis", "a", "ais", "b"]
def ly(m):
    octave = m // 12 - 4
    return NAMES[m % 12] + ("'" * octave if octave > 0 else "," * -octave)
notes = " ".join(ly(m) + DURATIONS[d] for m, d in tune)
folder = "figures/machine-listening/notation"
os.makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)
with open(f"{folder}/markov-tune.ly", "w") as f:
    f.write('\\include "../../notation/common.ily"\n'
            '% Written by the Markov tune cell in machine-listening.ipynb; do not edit by hand.\n'
            '\\score { \\new Staff { \\clef treble \\key c \\major \\time 4/4 ' + notes + ' \\bar "|." } }\n')
try:                                           # the SVG is shown by the image directive in the next cell
    subprocess.run(["bash", "figures/notation/render.sh", folder], check=True, capture_output=True)
except Exception:
    print("LilyPond is not available; the tune in LilyPond notation:", notes)

# 4. A plain tone for each note: four harmonics with an exponential decay, 100 beats per minute
sr, beat = 16000, 60 / 100
audio = []
for m, d in tune:
    t = np.arange(int(d * beat * sr)) / sr
    f0 = 440 * 2 ** ((m - 69) / 12)
    tone = sum(np.sin(2 * np.pi * f0 * h * t) / h for h in range(1, 5)) * np.exp(-3 * t / (d * beat))
    audio.append(tone)
audio = np.concatenate(audio)
display(Audio(audio / np.abs(audio).max(), rate=sr))

When analysing it, you can see that the tune is plausible: every pair of notes is followed by the third somewhere in the collection. So the steps, leaps and rhythms are those of the style. What it lacks is everything that spans more than three notes: phrases that return, a cadence halfway through, a shape that goes somewhere. A chain with a longer memory would copy longer fragments of the tunes it learned from, not invent new phrases. This is the gap that neural networks close.

solves the same prediction task as the Markov chain, but with a recurrent network whose state carries information about the whole tune so far, trained on tens of thousands of transcriptions. The large language models behind today’s chat systems predict the next token in the same way. Run the cell again with another seed and the chain writes another tune; it has no preference among them, and the choice of which to keep is the composer’s.
Audio-based generation systems produce the waveform directly. Research systems such as
and MusicGen showed that a written prompt like “upbeat funk with slap bass” could become sound, and commercial services such as
now deliver complete songs with vocals from a sentence of text.
is one of the few such systems with open weights, so it can run on a laptop. It does not predict samples: a neural audio codec first turns sound into a stream of discrete

The small model has about 300 million weights, which sounds like a lot, but the clips below took only seconds to generate on a laptop’s graphics card. The first clip comes from the prompt alone. The percussion model keeps the rhythm of the quartet and replaces every sound in it with a drum, because drums are all it can make. The vintage model keeps more of the pitch content and adds the surface noise and band-limited tone of old records. Neither model was told anything about jazz; what you hear is the training set playing through the input.

Remember that such systems do not actually know anything about music. They are based on processing huge collections of music and then adjusting their weights until they can predict how such music tends to continue. When prompted, they assemble new output that follows the statistical patterns they have absorbed. They do not replay any single piece from the training set and usually also produce new results each time they are triggered.
While such systems have proven to be very powerful, many of them are also based on learning from copyrighted music without asking for permission or paying the artists
. In 2024 major record labels took leading text-to-music services to court over the use of their catalogues, and that litigation is still running.

There is a cultural worry too: models trained mostly on commercially successful Western repertoire will also produce outputs that pull in the same direction. The result is a flood of generated similar-sounding music.

Today these systems are good at pastiche. They are good at generating a plausible 30-second lo-fi beat or a jingle in the style of 1980s synth-pop. They are much weaker when it comes to generating long-range form and breaking rules in the way that makes human-made music interesting. One can therefore think of them as idea-generating tools rather than as replacements.

Every system in this chapter was shaped by the music it learned from. This section asks what that music was, what other data are added to it, and what the choice of data means for the people whose music and listening it contains.
For decades, MIR researchers worked mostly with symbolic data, primarily
files. Most research now works with audio, which carries no symbols at all.
In addition to the data itself (MIDI, audio, etc.), we also have different types of
(how it was recorded or analysed) and
(who listened, and when). These supplementary data types give the music data its context.

Collecting diverse music data, metadata, paradata, and user data while respecting copyright, performers’ rights and privacy is one of the field’s standing problems. Researchers therefore lean on openly licensed recordings and documented datasets, and share down-sampled features or spectrograms when the audio itself cannot be shared.
Many systems add other data to the audio: lyrics to settle a mood, a score for exact pitches, video for the performer’s gestures. The MIR literature calls this
uses for perception through several senses. This book keeps multimodal for perception and speaks of data types here: a score and a recording are two kinds of data about one piece, not two senses.
Why is “multimodal data” a challenging term when working between music psychology and technology?
A core challenge when working with several data types is to synchronise them: audio, scores, lyrics and video run on different clocks and must be
before they can be compared. The second challenge is comparison between kinds of data, which many systems solve with
: lists of numbers from a trained model that place similar items, whether clips, lyric lines or images, close together.

As mentioned above, the datasets and the models built on them have social consequences. Field recordings, concerts and classroom sessions contain identifiable voices, so consent, licences and known limitations belong with every dataset. Training data skewed by genre, language, recording quality or Western labels give models that fail silently on the music they never saw, and since perception and meaning are culturally conditioned, a model trained on a narrow corpus misrepresents the practices outside it. The generative systems above add unresolved questions of artist consent, credit and compensation.

The same problem can be found when working with people’s data. There are huge potentials in using interactive music systems in health and well-being settings. However, information about people’s bodies and minds can be misused. Music-based therapy tools must be validated in proper trials before any benefit is claimed, as the music-therapy section of

Training large models also consumes large amounts of energy, so one should always keep the method proportionate to the question. And, for all sorts of work, one should be transparent about how AI-based tools are used.
Dig deeper: tools, datasets, and services
A few names you will meet in the literature and in practice; none of them is required for this course.

A critical look: does all music sound the same these days?

children.label: A critical look: does all music sound the same these days?

children.value: In 2012, a MIR study made the headlines: pop music was getting louder and more alike. The evidence came from audio features computed over hundreds of thousands of recordings.
is that popular music has become louder and less varied over the decades, in melody, harmony, and timbre.

is mixed. An analysis of nearly half a million tracks from 1955 to 2010 found that loudness rose steadily, that the range of timbres in use narrowed, and that transitions between pitches became more restricted over time

. However, a later study of 17,000 songs from the US charts, 1960 to 2010, described the same period differently: it found no steady decline in diversity but three stylistic revolutions, in 1964, 1983, and 1991, with a dip in diversity in the mid-1980s, when drum machines and synthesisers dominated, followed by a recovery as hip-hop arrived

is the same in both studies: chroma, timbre, and loudness features extracted from audio and tracked over time. So the disagreement comes from elsewhere: which recordings were included, which features were chosen, and what diversity is taken to mean. Each of those is a decision made by the analyst.

apply to any such claim. Descriptors are proxies for musical qualities, not the qualities themselves. Datasets over-represent charts and Western pop. And the sample of old music we compare against has been filtered by decades of forgetting, so the past always sounds more varied than it was.

One part of the claim holds and can be measured: recordings have become louder. The rest, that music got worse, is not something a feature extractor can answer. Machine listening can tell you what changed in the audio; whether the change is a loss is a judgement the perceiver still has to make.

Machine listening treats audio as data and runs one pipeline on it: clean the signal, extract features, separate sources, find events and sections, then ask a musical question of the result. Each stage borrows from an earlier chapter, from the spectrogram of acoustics to the auditory scene analysis of psychoacoustics, the periodicities of time and rhythm, and the pitch classes of harmony and melody. The Coltrane example showed that a tempo estimate and a chromagram describe the signal, not the music: the numbers need a listener to read them. Music information retrieval lets the machine decide rather than describe, with rule-based or learning-based systems, in real time or offline, and with artificial neural networks whose features no one chose. Generative AI turns the pipeline around, as a Markov chain over folk tunes, a transformer writing audio from a text prompt, or an autoencoder recasting one sound in another’s timbre, and every one of them speaks with the voice of its training data. That data, and the people whose music and listening it contains, raise the questions of consent, bias, energy and transparency that close the chapter. In the four levels of description the machine is strong at the signal and its digital representation, approximates perception where a perceptual model has been built in, and does not reach interpretation. The closing case showed that large-scale audio analysis confirms rising loudness but cannot settle whether music got worse: what changed is measurable, whether it is a loss is a judgement for the perceiver.

Walk through the pipeline of this chapter on a song you know well, from preprocessing through feature extraction, source separation and event detection, and name one earlier chapter that each stage draws on.
Give one low-level, one mid-level and one high-level audio feature, and say which perceptual or musical quality each approximates.
In the Coltrane example, why did the tempo estimate and the chromagram’s strong E and B need critical reading, and where does that place machine listening among the four levels of description?

A live accompaniment system and an archive-annotation project each need a machine listener. Which combination of rule-based or learning-based, real-time or offline, would you choose for each, and why?

The Markov tune, the MusicGen clips and the RAVE outputs were each shaped by their training data in a different way. Say how for each, and whose interests are at stake when a system is trained on copyrighted recordings without the artists’ consent.
